newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian needs external help for currency board.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian needs external help for currency board.

text.p: Bulgaria will not be able both to service its foreign debt and to introduce a currency board proposed by the IMF without external support, Central Bank Governor Lyubomir Filipov said on Friday.
"We can cover the levs in circulation and commercial banks' minimum reserves held at the central bank with the current foreign exchange reserves plus the gold," he told parliament.
"Then, however, there will be no money left to cover debt payments," he added.

He said preliminary estimates showed Bulgaria's foreign exchange and gold reserves currently stood at $950 million which needed to match 220 billion levs. The IMF has not specified so far the amount of support it would provide.
Foreign debt payments due next year top $1 billion.
An International Monetary Fund (IMF) technical mission was due in Sofia next week to prepare estimates for a currency board system, said Filipov, presenting the central bank position on the plan.
Currency boards, usually pegging the local currency to the dollar, have been used to defeat hyperinflation and restore confidence in countries such as Argentina, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia.

Filipov said there was a 10 to 20 percent chance of failure for the currency board, under which the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves.
Unlike other countries where the system has been applied, Bulgaria is burdened with undercapitalised banks and a huge internal debt.
"It is difficult to forsee what the impact of the currency board on other financial institutions would be, as we still do not know which type will it be," said Filipov.
Under milder versions, like the one applied in Argentina some central bank refinancing of commercial banks is possible in other cases like the on in Estonia it was curbed completely.

It is still not clear how some 600 billion lev in maturity payments due on government securities will be made next year. The IMF had proposed to rollover maturity payments until the interest rates fall under the effect of the currency board.

Bulgaria's biggest savings institution, the State Savings Bank, is likely to suffer severe liquidity problems under a currency board plan as 75 percent of its portfolio consisted of government securities, said its director Bistra Dimitrova.
Economists have warned that those banks which depend entirely on refinancing to solve their liquidity problems will have to be closed.
Filipov proposed to seek advice from local and foreign experts on the application of a currency board plan or its alternative.
He said that a fixed exchange rate was an intermediate stabilisation measure which should also be discussed.
The IMF had said however that a fixed rate would not solve Bulgaria's high interest problems.
"Under a currency board system the central bank will function not autonomously but automatically. It will operate regardless of budget gaps, be that for education or healthcare," said Filipov.
